title: Never Stop Driving #203: A 10-Hour Drive to Fix My Car

body_markdown:
At some point along the ten-hour journey I was taking just to get my carburetors tuned, I wondered: Where is the line between perseverance and obsession?


The car in need was my 1975 Ferrari Dino GT4,[the star-crossed restoration project](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/dino-finito-hdc-dino-final-update-tktk/) that I’ve been documenting in the pages of *Hagerty Drivers Club magazine* for five years. I passed the finish line a year ago—or so I imagined. The car reliably started and drove; the windows rolled up and down, the V-8 authoritatively ripped to the 7500-rpm redline. Even all the lights worked. After so much sweat and tears (not to mention hard-earned cash), I finally had the Dino of my dreams.


Cameron Neveu


Yet, there was a hiccup. When I pulled away from a stop, the V-8 stumbled two or three beats before roaring off. Annoying. I spent a year trying to correct this behavior myself by adjusting the four Weber carburetors. Better, but the engine still felt off. I concluded that I, the carburetor clueless, might require years of trial and error to land on the right combination of settings to make the car sing. I needed help.


The shops I hired in the Detroit area gave the car back with a pert, “Hey, it’s a fifty-year-old car; this is the way they were.” Maybe they were right. Was I chasing perfection that never existed?


Cameron Neveu


While on the phone with Dave North to get ignition replacement parts, I laid on my tale of woe. North runs a[small retirement business](https://www.marellidistributorservice.com/) in New Jersey that rebuilds distributors, and he daily drives an immaculate Ferrari 400i with 220,000 miles on the odo. There’s a guy, he said, who shares his shop and can definitely fix it. Why don’t you bring the car here? Something about the confidence in his voice hooked me. “When is his first opening?” I replied, “And can I watch him work?”


Six hundred miles later, I pulled into a nondescript industrial park in Whippany, New Jersey, and shook hands with Steve Markowski. He’s tall and thin with a welcoming face and bushy hair. At 49 years old, he’s also younger than my car. I’d met him on the phone once before, when he coached me through the tuning process. Now here I was, the student attending office hours.


Two equally frightening possibilities swirled in my head. One, that Markowski would immediately recognize something simple and obvious that I’d missed and fix the car in under an hour. I’ve been proven a fool so often that I could live with that. More worrying: We’d spend our allotted two days on the car and find that it’s as good as it’s going to get, which would leave me with a five-year wallet-sucking project that I just don’t like to drive.


Markowski dove in. He moved around the engine bay, swiftly verifying the timing setting and the ignition advance. Engine running, he agreed the motor was a little lazy to rev up. His ear was the primary tool at this stage, leading him to agree that the issue lied in the carburetors.


[The Weber carburetor](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/meet-mike-pierce-the-weber-whisperer/) is a wonder of engineering but also a bit of a Rubik’s cube. The basic body is a tube that necks down to increase air speed and draw fuel from a small reservoir. The challenge for any carburetor is to deliver the right amount of fuel across an engine’s wide operating range and constantly varying ambient conditions. The Weber does this via a handful of internal passages, adjustment screws, and small, perforated pieces called jets.


The jets come in different sizes that alter fuel delivery and how it mixes with the air. There are four different jets on each carburetor throat—one for each cylinder—and also an adjustable idle-mixture screw. Each jet affects the other, meaning there are at least 1000 possible jet recipes. Yikes.


Matt Tierney


Making matters even more complicated is the fact that five decades on from when this car was produced, Ferrari’s recommended tune for the carburetors is less than spot-on. For one thing, Markowski explained, the factory made running changes throughout the production run—and those changes weren’t always recorded in the service manual. Factor in the difference in modern fuel and the fact that my engine had been rebuilt, and it was no surprise that the factory settings were no longer the perfect point of reference. But where to try next?


Carb tuning is a version of the scientific method: Observe, form a theory, and then test that hypothesis. Observing means keeping every sense open—and having those senses keenly trained to notice what needs to be tweaked next. My amateur ears simply don’t have the hours of training required, which is why tuning the carbs proved so elusive and frustrating for me. Markowski, in contrast, literally grew up immersed in vintage cars. His father, Peter Markowski, started[Restoration and Performance Motorcars](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/restoration-and-performance-motorcars-turned-boys-ferrari-enthusiasm-into-family-business/) in Vermont in 1985, which is now one of the preeminent Ferrari shops in the Northeast. Steve has been tuning Ferrari engines since middle school.


Syd Cummings


Steve Markowski


Syd Cummings


Markowski’s first hypothesis was that the idle jets were the wrong size. I’d changed this small part dozens of times to no effect. Swapping a jet is a tedious process, wherein you unscrew a small brass jet the size of a Tic Tac from the side of each carburetor throat. Then, you run the engine while adjusting the air screws by ear. Then a test drive. Each experiment takes at least 45 minutes. It requires a kind of patience that’s hard to come by in our era of instant everything. Fortunately, Markowski has it. “If it takes five days, it takes five days,” he’d told me during our phone consult.


By late afternoon, the idle jet path had not yielded an improvement. What next? Markowski removed the three-inch-long brass cylinders, called emulsion tubes, which are drilled with holes along their length and create a fuel-air froth that slinks into the airflow. To him, the holes looked small. Perhaps emulsion tubes with larger holes might help?


Markowski got into what I call the zone. For about two hours, he worked at a startlingly quick pace, trying different tubes, going for a test drive, making another switch. Repeat. I just stood back and watched, mesmerized to observe a craftsman performing at his peak. By the end of the day, he thought he’d had it settled but wanted to sleep on the solution and see if any other idea emerged.


And there it was, the next morning: A crisp, stumble-free takeoff. Markowski and I drove around the neighborhood, making sure the engine ran properly at all operating temperatures. “These engines,” he commented, “are like living, breathing things that all have individualistic needs.”


I next spent the afternoon of a glorious fall day running the Dino through some nearby curvy roads. This was it, the experience I’d dreamed of some five years ago when I started this project. It’s cliché to say that fixing old cars is about the process. But it’s so true. The car hobby offers immense richness if you’re willing to stick with that process.


Cameron Neveu


Another thing: My little Dino reminds me that, even in the era of Artificial Intelligence, expertise matters. I’m sure an AI platform would have, if prompted, instantly spat out some recommendations for tuning my carbs. I’m equally sure they wouldn’t have worked. To get the right answer, I had to drive 10 hours and trust the right person. There’s comfort in the fact that some human knowledge remains truly special. It’s also getting harder to come by, as the old masters age out of their professions.


What that means, however, is that opportunity abounds for those starting their careers. Last week,[I wrote about](https://www.hagerty.com/media/never-stop-driving/never-stop-driving-202-the-car-trade-ai-cant-replace/) the recent *Barn Find Hunter* video where host Tom Cotter looked at the camera and described an AI-proof job restoring wood-bodied cars. And here we are again, talking about another specialized skill where the demand outstrips the supply. We all need to highlight that to the next generation. In the meantime, I’ll enjoy my now-perfect Dino (at least until the next time I decide that it isn’t perfect).


Never Stop Driving


Larry
